1. Verifying hardware virtualization

The installation commands in this article apply to different distributions and should not be run consecutively. On NixOS, maintain software and services through modules and Home Manager rather than directly editing /etc or dotfiles. AMD IOMMU is normally initialized by firmware and the kernel; iommu.strict=1 controls only the invalidation policy and is not an enable switch.
Before installing any software, confirm that the CPU supports hardware virtualization, the corresponding firmware extensions are enabled, and the kernel modules can load correctly.
1.1 Check CPU virtualization extensions
Intel platforms require VT-x (vmx); AMD platforms require AMD-V/SVM (svm).
If this returns 0, the CPU either does not support hardware virtualization or it is disabled in BIOS/UEFI.

3. User and permission configuration
libvirt controls access through UNIX sockets and PolicyKit. To let a non-root user manage virtual machines, add that user to the corresponding UNIX groups.
3.1 Add the user to the virtualization groups
Group name
Permission scope
Allows management of virtual machines, networks, and storage pools through the libvirt socket (/var/run/libvirt/libvirt-sock)
Allows access to the /dev/kvm device node to run QEMU processes with KVM acceleration
3.2 Make group changes take effect
usermod -aG changes the group membership loaded when a user logs in; existing shell sessions do not automatically inherit the new groups.

Group changes must take effect If you run virsh list --all before the group changes take effect, you will receive Failed to connect to the hypervisor or Permission denied. Make sure the current session has membership in the libvirt group.
3.3 Verify permissions
If virsh list --all runs without sudo and returns an empty list, the permissions are configured correctly.

4.2 The modular daemon architecture
In modern distributions (Fedora 35+, Ubuntu 24.04+, Arch Linux), libvirt has been split from a monolithic libvirtd into multiple specialized daemons:
Traditional daemon
Modern modular replacement
Responsibility
libvirtd (monolithic)
QEMU/KVM virtual-machine management
Virtual network management (NAT, bridge, DHCP)
Storage pool management (dir, LVM, iSCSI, and others)
Host device management (PCI, USB, and others)
Key/password management (Ceph, iSCSI CHAP, and others)
Host network interface management
Unified proxy entry point that routes requests to the appropriate module
Check which architecture is in use:
With the modular architecture, virsh uri outputs qemu:///system, which is actually handled by virtqemud
The monolithic architecture also outputs qemu:///system, but it is handled by libvirtd
From the user's perspective, virsh and virt-manager make exactly the same API calls with either architecture; the difference is transparent.

Host to virtual machine: the host can directly ping 192.0.2.x

Verify that IP forwarding is enabled
KVM NAT networking depends on the host's IP forwarding. Check its status:
If the value is 0, libvirt normally enables it automatically when starting the default network. However, disabling it manually may prevent virtual machines from reaching external networks.
6. Verifying the installation

This section uses CirrOS 0.6.2, a historical smoke-test image; the x86_64 disk file listed in the official directory is approximately 20 MiB. MD5SUMS can check only for accidental transfer corruption, not provide strong source authentication. Check the signatures and strong-checksum chain available for the actual release. Do not use this kind of test image or its publicly known default password for externally exposed services. Paths read by system QEMU must also satisfy security policies and directory permissions; --graphics none does not automatically make an arbitrary guest provide a serial login.
Use a CirrOS test image for end-to-end verification. CirrOS is a minimal Linux distribution of only about 12MB, designed specifically for OpenStack/KVM testing.

6.4 Clean up the test virtual machine
virsh destroy <name>: forcibly stop the virtual machine, similar to cutting power; data not yet written to disk may be lost. It does not delete the virtual-machine definition or disks.
virsh shutdown <name>: send an ACPI shutdown signal to the guest for a graceful shutdown; the guest needs an ACPI service installed
virsh undefine <name>: remove the virtual-machine configuration from the libvirt database; it does not delete disk files. Add --remove-all-storage to also delete the associated storage volumes.

7.2 Configure the VM storage directory

pool-define-as creates a persistent definition, which is then activated by pool-start. pool-create-as creates only a transient pool, so do not assume it can autostart. System QEMU needs actual directory-traversal and file read/write permissions; home directories are often restricted by permissions or security policies. Choose an authorized storage directory rather than using chmod to open up the entire home directory.
Create a dedicated directory for virtual-machine disks and ISO images:
7.3 Configure remote management (optional)

Prefer an SSH tunnel: the remote account needs both SSH authentication and group or polkit authorization for the remote system libvirt socket. Permission to log in over SSH alone does not grant libvirt management access.

TLS management requires a CA, server and client certificates, correct hostname verification, private-key permissions, access control, and the appropriate socket configuration. Historical monolithic-daemon configuration keys include listen_tls, tls_port, key_file, cert_file, and ca_file. For socket activation or virtproxyd deployments, follow the official documentation for the architecture in use; editing the old libvirtd.conf alone is insufficient.

The historical combination of plaintext TCP listen_tcp and unauthenticated auth_tcp grants full management capability to anyone who can reach the port; it should not be the default even on a "trusted internal network." TLS commonly uses port 16514, while plaintext TCP commonly uses 16509. The port number does not prove that a connection is authenticated or encrypted.
Summary

Whether the default NAT network is defined, started, or configured to autostart depends on the distribution's installation and existing state. NAT provides outbound forwarding, not complete security isolation; guests can usually still access the host's virtual bridge and other guests on the same network. The example subnet uses a documentation range to illustrate the topology. Replace it with a nonconflicting RFC1918 private network when creating a real network.
After configuration, verify each of the following conditions. The commands in this article have not been run:
KVM hardware acceleration is ready
The QEMU + libvirt software stack is installed
User permissions are configured correctly, allowing virtual-machine management without sudo
libvirtd, or the equivalent modular daemons, starts automatically at boot
The default NAT network is available
